title: 1956 Hawker Hunter multiple aircraft accident
summary: Eight RAF Hawker Hunter F.1 jet fighters from the Day Fighter Leader Squadron conducting a 4x4 dogfight exercise at 45,000 feet departed RAF West Raynham on February 8, 1956. By 11:00 a.m., weather at the home airfield had deteriorated with poor visibility, and the formation was diverted to nearby RAF Marham for a visual approach. Visibility suddenly reduced to near zero during approach with only 10 minutes of fuel remaining. Six of the eight aircraft were lost when pilots descended trying to locate the ground. Engines flamed out from fuel exhaustion as the aircraft descended below safe altitudes, and pilots ejected. One pilot (WW635) was killed when his aircraft crashed. The Board of Inquiry determined that sudden weather deterioration was the primary cause and the diversion to Marham on assumption of visual landing was an error of judgment.

title: TWA 400
summary: As TWA Flight 400 became airborne, a sharp yaw developed at 100 feet. A fire warning light for the number one engine illuminated, though the warning bell did not sound. The first officer throttled down the engine while the captain, not seeing the light, pulled the mixture to idle cutoff. This prevented the autofeather system from engaging due to throttle lever position. The unfeathered propeller created insurmountable drag, causing the aircraft to crash 1,690 feet past the runway. All 22 of 36 occupants died.

title: Northwest Orient Airlines 2
summary: Northwest Airlines Flight 2, a Boeing 377 Stratocruiser, departed Seattle-Tacoma on April 2, 1956. Shortly after takeoff, the first officer retracted the wing flaps and the aircraft suddenly began to buffet violently and roll left. The captain, believing an asymmetric wing flap condition had developed, found the aircraft uncontrollable and decided to ditch in Puget Sound. All 40 occupants initially survived the ditching, but four passengers and one flight attendant died from hypothermia in the 42-degree water before rescue. Investigation revealed the flight engineer had failed to close the engine cowl flaps for takeoff.

title: Braathens SAFE 253
summary: The de Havilland Heron crashed into Hummelfjell mountain at 1,350 meters altitude in Norway on 7 November 1956 at 9:50 while descending with icing and a downdraft. The aircraft was en route from Trondheim to Oslo when it began experiencing rapid atmospheric icing around Røros which exceeded the capacity of the ice protection system. Combined with a downdraft, the aircraft lost sufficient lift to remain airborne. The pilots turned the aircraft around to return to Trondheim, but the icing accumulated so rapidly that the aircraft lost altitude very quickly. Ice covered the windshield and radio antenna, disabling radio communication and navigation. The crew was unaware they were flying over the mountain when the aircraft struck terrain at 300 km/h, traveling tail-first.
